cards.title: E. F. Codd
cards.prompt: The 1970 paper that founded the relational model argues from one worked example. Who wrote it, which IBM site was he at, what was the example, and what did he name the defect he found in it?
cards.body: E. F. Codd, IBM Research Laboratory, San Jose. He was not selling a query language; he was naming three data dependencies. His example is parts and projects, drawn as five legal hierarchies, and he shows a program written for one of them “will fail on at least three of the remaining structures.” He called it access path dependence.
cards.answer: E. F. Codd, at IBM's San Jose research laboratory. The example is parts and projects, arranged as five hierarchies; the defect is “access path dependence,” and a program written for one hierarchy fails on at least three of the others.

cards.title: The terminal at Downey
cards.sub: 14 August 1968 · Rockwell Space Division, Downey, California
cards.prompt: Three companies staffed the team that built ICS and DL/I. Name them and the headcount each contributed, then say what the terminal at Downey printed when the system went live, on what hardware, and on what date.
cards.body: 1966: 12 from IBM, 10 from North American Rockwell, 3 from Caterpillar Tractor. Rockwell had won the bid to launch the first spacecraft to the moon and needed its bills of material automated. ICS was installed April 1968; the first “IMS READY” reached an IBM 2740 terminal on 14 August 1968.
cards.answer: IBM (12), North American Rockwell (10) and Caterpillar Tractor (3), from 1966. The message was “IMS READY,” on an IBM 2740 terminal at the Rockwell Space Division in Downey, California, 14 August 1968.

cards.title: Section 1.2.3
cards.prompt: Where exactly can you read the original argument that a tree-structured database welds application programs to the storage layout? Give the paper, the journal, the volume and issue, the month, and the numbered section — the section number is not the one people quote.
cards.body: E. F. Codd, “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks,” Communications of the ACM, Volume 13, Number 6, June 1970, pp. 377–387. The section is 1.2.3, “Access Path Dependence” — not 1.1.3. Codd's own phrase for the workload in it is “the parts explosion problem”: the walk IMS was built to make cheap.
cards.answer: Codd, “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks,” CACM vol. 13 no. 6, June 1970, pp. 377–387, section 1.2.3 “Access Path Dependence.”

cards.title: The table is the query
cards.sub: 1968 → today · hierarchical storage to single-table design
cards.prompt: IMS's bargain is sold again today under different names. State the bargain in one sentence, name the modern stores that sell it, and give the one dated number that shows how hard the bargain is to unwind once it is running.
cards.body: The bargain: put the access path into the stored layout, and one traversal becomes nearly free while every other question becomes a new program. Wide-column and single-table designs resell it — the table is the query. How hard to unwind: in 1998, thirty years on, IBM counted “over 90 percent of the top worldwide companies” still running IMS daily.
cards.answer: One access path made cheap in the physical layout, everything else expensive. Cassandra/ScyllaDB partition-plus-clustering keys and DynamoDB single-table designs sell the same trade. The number: in 1998 IBM counted over 90 percent of the top worldwide companies in ten named sectors still running IMS for daily operations.
